nameStory: The American Dog Tick earned its name because it's commonly found feeding on domestic dogs across North America. While it's also called the 'wood tick' for its preference for wooded areas, the 'dog tick' name stuck because pet owners frequently discover these unwelcome hitchhikers on their furry companions after walks in the woods.
description: The American Dog Tick is one of New England's most recognizable hard-bodied ticks, with a tough, shield-like back that feels almost plastic when touched. These blood-sucking arachnids are about the size of a small apple seed when unfed, but can swell to the size of a grape when engorged with blood. They're reddish-brown with distinctive white or yellowish markings on their backs, making them easier to spot than many other tick species. Like all ticks, they have eight legs and are more closely related to spiders than insects.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Hard, oval-shaped body with a tough, shield-like back that feels rigid and smooth like plastic when touched, unlike soft ticks which feel leathery

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Distinctive white or pale yellow ornate patterns on a reddish-brown background, creating a decorative appearance that's unique among New England ticks

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Unfed adults are about 3-5mm (roughly the size of a small apple seed), but engorged females can balloon to 15mm (grape-sized) and feel firm yet squishy

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Climbs onto grass tips and low shrubs with front legs extended, waiting to grab onto passing animals - a behavior called 'questing'

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: When handled, feels much harder and more rigid than soft-bodied ticks, with a glossy surface that doesn't compress easily

habitat: American Dog Ticks thrive in grassy fields, woodland edges, and shrubland throughout New England, particularly in areas where tall grasses meet wooded borders. They prefer open, sunny areas with low vegetation rather than deep forest interiors, making them common along hiking trails, old fields, and suburban areas where yards meet wild spaces. You'll often encounter them in dog parks, recreational trails, and anywhere domestic animals or wildlife create well-traveled paths.

seasonality.spring: Peak activity begins in April and May when adults emerge to seek blood meals and mates. This is when you're most likely to find them questing on grass tips and low vegetation.
seasonality.summer: Most active period from June through July when adults are actively seeking hosts for feeding and reproduction. Engorged females will drop off to lay thousands of eggs in leaf litter.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases significantly, though some stragglers may still be found into early fall. Newly hatched larvae may be present but are extremely small and difficult to spot.
seasonality.winter: Adults become dormant and hide in leaf litter and soil. No surface activity occurs during cold months, making this the safest season for tick-free outdoor activities.

funFact: An American Dog Tick can survive for over two years without eating a single meal, patiently waiting on a blade of grass with its arms outstretched like a tiny hitchhiker until the perfect host walks by.
confusionNotes: Often confused with deer ticks (blacklegged ticks), but American Dog Ticks are larger, have distinctive white markings, and feel much harder to the touch. Remember: 'White spots = dog tick, all dark = deer tick.' Deer ticks are also much smaller and prefer wooded areas while dog ticks like open, grassy spaces.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'American Dog Tick,' these arachnids will readily feed on humans, cats, and many wild animals - they're not picky eaters. Importantly, while they can carry Rocky Mountain spotted fever and tularemia, they do NOT transmit Lyme disease, which is exclusively spread by deer ticks in New England.
compareHints: American Dog Ticks are much more common in New England than their cousin the Winter Tick, which primarily feeds on moose and deer rather than dogs and humans. While both have the characteristic hard shield, Winter Ticks lack the distinctive white ornate markings and are typically found on large wildlife rather than pets. American Dog Ticks also prefer the warmer months while Winter Ticks are most active during fall and early winter.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Winter ticks differ from their close relative, the American dog tick, primarily in their seasonal activity and host preferences.
